o: Tasks must be done in order, one per day, optionally inserting rest days; the same task type cannot repeat within `space` days. Track the last completion day per type: when task t is due on day cur+1 but was last done on day d, we must wait until d + space + 1. Example 1 with space=3 stretches the schedule to 9 days; Example 2 to 6. A single simulation with a hash map gives the answer in O(n).
k: Greedy simulation is optimal: never idle unless forced, because idling early can't help future constraints.
Next allowed day for type t is last[t] + space + 1; the schedule day advances to max(cur + 1, that bound).
Only the LAST completion day of each type matters — a hash map keyed by task type suffices.

a.i: Maintain `cur` = current day and last[type] = day that type was last executed. For each task in order, jump cur to max(cur + 1, last[t] + space + 1), execute, and record last[t] = cur. This is a tight lower bound matched constructively, hence optimal.
s: For each task t: cur = max(cur + 1, last.get(t, -inf) + space + 1); last[t] = cur.
a.t: O(n) — one pass; each task triggers O(1) map work.
a.sp: O(u) — u = number of distinct task types.

w: One approach is optimal; a day-by-day simulation (incrementing through breaks) also works but is needlessly slower in code though still O(n) amortized. Pitfalls: off-by-one on the cooldown — the gap must be at least `space` FULL days between completions, hence last + space + 1; and using 32-bit integers (the answer can exceed 2^31 with n = 10^5 and large spaces). Follow-up: what if tasks could be reordered? That is LC 621's variant with a different greedy (frequency + slots).
